facts.text: In 1895, while testing a covered glass tube in his lab in Germany, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered rays he called X, meaning unknown.
X-rays passed through flesh more easily than through bone, so Röntgen could see the bones of a hand.
Röntgen's first published X-ray image showed his wife's hand, with her bones and her wedding ring visible; it amazed the public.
Within months of the discovery, doctors were using X-rays to find broken bones and bullets in patients.
In 1896 Thomas Edison showed a fluoroscope, a viewer with a glowing screen; crowds lined up to look at their own bones.
Edison's assistant Clarence Dally held his hands in front of X-ray tubes for hours at a time while testing them.
Like many researchers of the time, Dally expected his radiation burns to heal with rest; instead he lost both arms and died in 1904.
After Dally's injuries, Edison stopped working with X-rays.
Ian Donald, a Glasgow doctor, worked with engineer Tom Brown to adapt an industrial machine for finding flaws in metal into a medical ultrasound scanner.
Ultrasound sends sound waves too high for human hearing into the body and builds pictures from the returning echoes.
Donald's 1958 report in The Lancet, written with two colleagues, contained the first ultrasound images of a baby in the womb.
Ultrasound is poor at imaging bone and air-filled organs such as the lungs, and it uses no X-rays.
On ordinary X-ray photographs, bones show up in fine detail, but the soft brain looks like fog.
Engineer Godfrey Hounsfield built the first CT scanner; it sent X-ray beams through the head from many angles and a computer turned the readings into slices.
The first CT scan of a patient was made in 1971 at a London hospital; it revealed a tumor in a woman's brain.
CT uses X-rays, a form of ionizing radiation; the risk of harm grows as a person receives more scans over a lifetime.
Around 1974, a team in St. Louis built an early PET scanner; Michael Phelps and Edward Hoffman were among its members.
Before a PET scan, patients receive a tracer, most often a form of sugar carrying a small amount of radioactive material.
Cancer cells use sugar faster than healthy cells, so PET shows how tissue is working rather than only its shape.
In 1977 Raymond Damadian's team made the first MRI image of a human body, a rough picture of a volunteer's chest that took nearly five hours.
MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves instead of X-rays and is especially good at showing soft tissue.
Patients must stay very still during an MRI scan, because movement blurs the image; modern scanners are much faster than the first one.
In 1990 Seiji Ogawa, working at Bell Laboratories in the United States, showed that MRI could detect how much oxygen the blood carries.

Active brain areas receive extra oxygen-rich blood, so functional MRI can show the brain at work; early human studies (1991 to 1992) used flashing lights, and later studies used tasks such as hand movements.

notes: Years used as entry labels: 1895, 1896, 1958, 1971, mid-1970s (around 1974), 1977, 1990.
